---
title: "Governance"
subtitle: "Pay or Restore? Assumptions, sensitivity, limitations and checks"
---

```{r setup}
#| include: false
source("R/00_params.R"); source("R/01_utils.R"); source("R/90_theme.R")
library(dplyr); library(gt)
wa <- read_result("walkaway")
sens <- read_result("sensitivity")
diag <- read_result("diagnostics")
rep <- read_result("reputation")
cal <- sens$calib
mc <- read_result("mc_drivers")
be <- rep$break_even
be_of <- \(f) be$eta_star[be$firm == f]
oat3 <- sens$oat[3, ]
bp <- P$bargaining
```

*All money is in $M and all values are illustrative.*

This page records what the analysis assumes, how much the answer moves when those assumptions change, and the checks that the numbers are computed correctly. It is the place to start before using any figure from this site in a real decision.

## Assumptions register

```{r}
#| label: tbl-assumptions
#| tbl-cap: "Assumptions register. Each assumption has an owner and a trigger for review."
rng <- \(v) paste(unlist(INPUT_SPEC[[v]]$par)[c(1, 3)], collapse = "–")
values <- c(
  c = sprintf("$%gM per day (range %s)", BASE$c, rng("c")),
  T_r = sprintf("%g days (range %s)", BASE$T_r, rng("T_r")),
  b = sprintf("%.2f (Beta(8, 2))", BASE$b),
  q = sprintf("%.2f (Beta(17, 3))", BASE$q),
  s = sprintf("%.2f (Beta(2, 18)); penalty %g × ransom", BASE$s, BASE$kappa),
  `p_np|p_p` = sprintf("%.2f if we refuse; %.2f if we pay", BASE$p_np, BASE$p_p),
  prior = sprintf("Median $%gM, log-sd %g; incident-to-incident log-sd %g", bp$prior_median, bp$prior_sdlog, bp$incident_sdlog),
  eta = sprintf("%g (tested %g to %g)", P$reputation$eta_base, min(ETA_FINE), max(ETA_FINE)),
  p0 = sprintf("%s a year (%s to %s on the slider)", fmt_pct(P$reputation$p0_base), fmt_pct(min(P0_GRID)), fmt_pct(max(P0_GRID))),
  posted = "One take-it-or-leave-it demand per incident",
  crew = sprintf("One crew over %d years", P$reputation$years)
)
readr::read_csv(file.path(PROJECT_ROOT, "data", "assumptions_register.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(value = values[param]) |>
  select(id, assumption, value, basis, owner, review_trigger) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(id = "ID", assumption = "Assumption", value = "Value", basis = "Basis",
             owner = "Owner", review_trigger = "Review trigger") |>
  cols_width(id ~ px(50), value ~ px(200)) |>
  gt_board()
```

::: {.reader-note}
**How to read the table.** Each row is one assumption the results depend on. The value column gives the number used and, where relevant, the range tested. The basis says whether it is a firm judgment, a simplification, or anchored to a published source. The owner is the executive who should sign off on the value, and the review trigger is the event that should prompt an update.

**What the table tells you.** Almost every input is a judgment that the firm would replace with its own figures. The two that matter most are restore time (A2) and backup credibility (A3), both of which a restore test can measure directly. The targeting response (A8) and the attack rate (A8b) drive the reputation result and have the weakest evidence behind them.
:::

## Sensitivity

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sensitivity
#| tbl-cap: !expr paste0("Walk-away point when one input moves to its 10th or 90th percentile, all others at base. Base walk-away point ", fmt_m(wa$R_base, 2), ".")
sens$oat |>
  select(label, low, high, R_low, R_high, swing) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(label = "Input", low = "Low value", high = "High value",
             R_low = "Walk-away at low ($M)", R_high = "Walk-away at high ($M)", swing = "Swing ($M)") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(low, high), n_sigfig = 2) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(R_low, R_high, swing), decimals = 2) |>
  tab_spanner("Input range", c(low, high)) |>
  gt_board()
```

::: {.reader-note}
**How to read the table.** Each row moves one input from a low value to a high value: the points below which 10% and 90% of its range fall. Everything else stays at base. The next two columns give the walk-away point at each end, and the swing is the gap between them. Rows are sorted with the biggest swing at the top.

**What the table tells you.** Restore time moves the walk-away point by `r fmt_m(sens$oat$swing[1], 2)`, more than any other input, followed by backup credibility at `r fmt_m(sens$oat$swing[sens$oat$input == "b"], 2)`. Better information on both, for example from a full restore test, is the most valuable input the board can buy. `r oat3$label`, which the crew's tooling sets, is the third-largest swing: even after paying, the platform stays down for about `r BASE$d_pay + BASE$T_d` days at base.
:::

```{r}
#| label: tbl-calibration
#| tbl-cap: "Share of simulated incidents in which paying is the cheaper path, under this firm's ranges and under market-typical restore times."
cal |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(case = "Ranges", T_r_median = "Median restore (days)", T_r_range = "Restore range (days)",
             b_mean = "Average backup credibility", R_median = "Median walk-away ($M)", pay_share = "Pay share") |>
  fmt_number(columns = T_r_median, decimals = 1) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(b_mean, R_median), decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = pay_share, decimals = 0) |>
  gt_board()
```

::: {.reader-note}
**How to read the table.** Each row is a Monte Carlo run of `r fmt_num(N_MC, 0)` simulated incidents, each with its own inputs and a random demand. The first row uses this firm's ranges. The second shrinks restore times so that the median is `r P$monte_carlo$market_T_r_median` days and makes backups work about `r fmt_pct(cal$b_mean[2])` of the time. The last column is the share of incidents in which paying is cheaper than restoring.

**What the table tells you.** With this firm's ranges, paying is the cheaper path in `r fmt_pct(cal$pay_share[1])` of incidents; with faster restores and stronger backups, in `r fmt_pct(cal$pay_share[2])`. Reported market payment rates lie between the two runs, so the model brackets the market rather than matching it. The high first figure reflects this firm's slow restores: the same model with market-like recovery pays far less often.
:::

The simulated pay share is high because this firm restores slowly: its median restore time is `r fmt_num(cal$T_r_median[1], 1)` days, against roughly a week for most victims ([Sophos 2025](https://assets.sophos.com/X24WTUEQ/at/9brgj5n44hqvgsp5f5bqcps/sophos-state-of-ransomware-2025.pdf)). At the base demand of `r fmt_m(D_BASE)`, paying on day one is cheaper in `r fmt_pct(mc$summary$p_pay_at_base_demand)` of draws. The market payment rate was 23% in Q3 2025 ([Coveware](https://coveware.com/2025/10/insider-threats-loom-while-ransom-payment-rates-plummet/)), fell to a new record low in Q2 2026 ([Coveware](https://coveware.com/2026/07/adverse-cyber-extortions-are-more-common-than-commonly-advised/)), and nearly 80% of Q3 2026 incidents were resolved without payment ([Coveware](https://coveware.com/2026/10/the-silent-ransom-group-leak-shows-why-paying-for-silence-fails/)). That rate lies between the two runs, about `r round(0.23 / cal$pay_share[2], 1)` times the market-calibration figure. Observed payment rates also reflect insurance, law-enforcement involvement and corporate policy, which this model leaves out.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-demand-spread
#| tbl-cap: "Share of the variation in the pay-or-not decision explained by each input, as the spread of demands widens. The median demand and all other draws are held fixed."
sbs <- mc$shares_by_sdlog
sbs |>
  filter(input %in% c("E_T", "T_r", "b", "D")) |>
  mutate(input = factor(input, levels = c("E_T", "T_r", "b", "D"))) |>
  select(sdlog, pay_share, input, share) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = input, values_from = share) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(sdlog = "Demand spread (log-sd)", pay_share = "Pay share", E_T = "Expected outage time",
             T_r = "Restore time", b = "Backup credibility", D = "Ransom demand") |>
  tab_spanner("Share of variation in the pay decision", c(E_T, T_r, b, D)) |>
  fmt_number(columns = sdlog, decimals = 1) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = c(pay_share, E_T, T_r, b, D), decimals = 0) |>
  gt_board()
```

::: {.reader-note}
**How to read the table.** Each row reruns the `r fmt_num(N_MC, 0)` simulated incidents with demands spread more or less widely around the same median. The first column measures that spread: `r fmt_num(min(sbs$sdlog), 1)` is the site's moderate assumption, and `r fmt_num(max(sbs$sdlog), 1)` is closer to the spread of published payments across all victims. The next column is how often paying is cheaper. The rest show how much of the yes-or-no decision each input explains on its own.

**What the table tells you.** The ranking flips as demands vary more widely. At the moderate spread, expected outage time explains `r fmt_pct(sbs$share[sbs$sdlog == min(sbs$sdlog) & sbs$input == "E_T"])` of the decision and the demand `r fmt_pct(sbs$share[sbs$sdlog == min(sbs$sdlog) & sbs$input == "D"])`; at the widest, the demand explains `r fmt_pct(sbs$share[sbs$sdlog == max(sbs$sdlog) & sbs$input == "D"])`. What holds at every spread is structural: restore time sets the walk-away point, and the demand only tests it. The pay share also falls as demands spread out, because more of them land far above the walk-away point.
:::

## Limitations

- **Synthetic firm.** Every cost and probability is illustrative; a real decision needs the firm's own outage cost, restore-test results and leak exposure.
- **Posted demand.** The crew names one price. Negotiated discounts exist, so treating the demand as final overstates the cost of paying.
- **No cyber insurance.** Insurance would cover part of the outage and possibly the ransom, which shifts the walk-away point.
- **One crew.** The model has a single crew that learns from our history. Several crews, or crews that share intelligence, would change how fast reputation builds.
- **Leak cost is fixed.** It does not depend on the number or sensitivity of the records taken.
- **The targeting response is uncertain.** The reputation result holds only if crews favor known payers: above about `r fmt_num(be_of("typical"), 2)` for our firm and `r fmt_num(be_of("fragile"), 2)` for the fragile firm; see the [Decision Map & Reputation](map-reputation.qmd#the-assumption-everything-rests-on) page.
- **The crew learns about our walk-away point, not our policy.** A firm that never pays looks like one with a low walk-away point, so its demand keeps falling instead of the crew moving on.
- **The staged path needs time.** Restoring first and paying only if backups fail assumes the firm can negotiate while restoring; leak deadlines or rising demands can remove that option.
- **Sanctions are a cost, not a bar.** A known sanctions link would rule out payment entirely rather than add a penalty.
- **Outage cost is constant per day.** In practice client churn accelerates after the first week, which would make restore time matter even more.
- **The decryptor works fully or not at all.** Partial decryption would leave some restore effort even after paying.

## Diagnostics

```{r}
#| label: tbl-diagnostics
#| tbl-cap: "Checks run by the pipeline on every build."
diag |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(check = "Check", result = "Result", detail = "Detail") |>
  tab_style(cell_text(color = "#1a7f37", weight = "bold"), cells_body(columns = result, rows = result == "Pass")) |>
  tab_style(cell_text(color = "#b42318", weight = "bold"), cells_body(columns = result, rows = result != "Pass")) |>
  gt_board()
```

::: {.reader-note}
**How to read the table.** Each row is one automatic check that runs every time the analysis is rebuilt. The result column shows whether it passed, and the detail column gives the evidence: the size of any error, the number of cases checked, or the values compared. A failure stops the build, so a published page should never show one.

**What the table tells you.** `r sum(diag$result == "Pass")` of `r nrow(diag)` checks pass. The formula matches an event-by-event simulation, the interactive map uses exactly the same formula as the R code, the simulation results move smoothly as the attack rate changes, and the main ranking of drivers does not depend on the random seed. Together they show that the numbers follow from the stated assumptions; they cannot show that the assumptions are right.
:::

To rebuild everything, run `Rscript R/run_all.R` and then `quarto render`; the [Reproducibility](reproducibility.qmd) page has the full steps.
